stem: A client with a serious progressive illness already has an advance directive and asks how a POLST or similar portable medical-order form differs. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: It provides medical orders that clinicians can act on immediately in an emergency in addition to an advance directive; availability and form depend on the state or jurisdiction.
options.B: It is primarily intended for healthy adults planning far ahead and replaces the advance directive once completed.
options.C: It records values for later discussion but does not function as a medical order during an emergency.
options.D: A single standard POLST form should be used nationwide because state-specific availability and requirements do not affect these orders.

rationale: NIH/NIA explains that POLST/MOLST forms provide guidance about medical care that healthcare professionals can act on immediately in an emergency and that they serve as medical orders in addition to an advance directive. They are typically created when a person is near the end of life or critically ill and understands the specific decisions that may need to be made. NIA also directs patients to check with their state health department because availability varies by state. Thus, POLST/MOLST does not replace an advance directive and is not merely a values document for future discussion.
educational_objective: Distinguish an advance directive from a POLST/MOLST-type portable medical order: the latter provides immediately actionable medical orders for seriously ill patients and supplements rather than replaces the advance directive.
source_organization: National Institutes of Health, National Institute on Aging (NIA)
source_document_title: Advance Care Planning: Advance Directives for Health Care
source_version_date: Content reviewed 2022-10-31; page current and rechecked 2026-08-16

source_claim_supported: NIA states POLST/MOLST forms can be acted on immediately in an emergency, serve as medical orders in addition to an advance directive, are typically used near end of life or critical illness, and may not be available in every state.

source_original.stem: A client with serious progressive illness already has an advance directive and asks how a POLST or similar portable medical-order form differs. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: It turns current treatment preferences into actionable medical orders in addition to an advance directive; state availability varies.
options.B: It is mainly for healthy adults planning far ahead and replaces the advance directive once it is signed.
options.C: It records values for future discussion but does not function as a medical order during an emergency.
options.D: Use a standard POLST form across states because the resulting clinical orders remain portable once they are signed by the appropriate clinician.

source_original.rationale: NIH/NIA explains that POLST/MOLST forms provide guidance that healthcare professionals can act on immediately in an emergency and serve as medical orders in addition to an advance directive. They are generally used for people who are seriously ill or near the end of life, and patients should check their state because availability and form vary.

correction_summary: Retained the construct and key. Tightened the wording to NIA's exact distinction: immediately actionable medical orders that supplement an advance directive, with state-dependent availability. Rewrote the portability distractor to avoid implying a universal interstate portability rule not established by the source. Verified exact NCSBN Appendix A advance-directives mapping on printed p. 20.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Advance care planning — POLST/MOLST versus advance directives
audit_findings.source_authority: Official NIH/NIA patient guidance; NCSBN used for blueprint only.
audit_findings.currentness: NIA content review date is October 31, 2022 but the page remains live as current NIA guidance and was rechecked 2026-08-16; no newer conflicting NIA guidance identified.
audit_findings.exact_locator: NIA's POLST/MOLST subsection directly supports immediate actionability, medical-order status, typical serious-illness context, and state availability.
audit_findings.claim_audit: Removed any unsupported universal interstate portability rule; final claims stay within NIA wording.

distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because NIA describes POLST/MOLST for critical illness/near end of life and says it supplements an advance directive.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because NIA explicitly describes it as a medical order actionable in an emergency.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because NIA directs clients to check state availability rather than use one universal form.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A correctly distinguishes function, relationship to advance directives, and state variation.
audit_findings.cueing: All options address the same document-function construct; no unrelated distractor or numerical cue.
audit_findings.blueprint: NCSBN 2026 Appendix A printed p.20 explicitly includes Advance Directives/Self-Determination/Life Planning.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Adversarial review focused on state portability and avoided converting state availability into a stronger legal portability claim.
